articles.body:
Oil prices rose amid reports Thursday that the White House is weighing new strike options on Iran, less than a month before the November elections.

Brent crude, the global benchmark , increased to $104.60 per barrel with a 4.4 percent jump Thursday morning. The U.S. benchmark, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) , jumped 3.91 percent and settled at $92.19 per barrel.

The national average for a gallon gas in the U.S. sat at $4.36, lower than last week’s $4.41, according to AAA .

U.S. officials told Axios Wednesday that the Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command (Centcom) to wrap up its preparations to resume combat operations in Iran. No final decisions have been made, but the strikes are expected to target Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear facilities.

The Atlantic first reported the Trump administration could resume operations in Iran ahead of the midterms, which could be seen as something of a victory for Republicans hoping to keep their majorities in Congress.

“It would make the president look like he got a win and that gas prices would start going down,” a Republican familiar with the deliberations told The Atlantic.

An Israeli official told Axios that while discussions about the U.S. resuming strikes on Iran “increased,” any attacks prior to the midterms have not been ruled out.

“After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly,” the official said.

The White House told The Hill that “all options” are available for President Trump to resume strikes, adding that the U.S. “is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing.”

The U.S. military has maintained a naval blockade at Iranian ports in the strait, which Iran effectively closed after the conflict began Feb. 28. The closure and tit-for-tat attacks have caused oil prices to surge , given the passage transports roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas.

Trump has often talked about resuming strikes after the election, repeating his threat that Iran could be annihilated in his address to the United Nations General Assembly last month. He has since suggested that it could happen before the election.

The president has also said that while the conflict “should help” Republican odds of keeping control of Congress, “ it’s possible ” that it could jeopardize those chances.

Israeli sources noted to Axios that the strikes could also happen before Israel’s elections later this month.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is up for reelection and has faced growing opposition as Israelis accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack that killed more than 1,000 Israelis. Political opponents have called Netanyahu’s coalition the “massacre government,” The Associated Press reported .

articles.title: ‘Chances remain high for a historic event’: El Niño is strengthening, forecasters warn
articles.summary: A strong, long-lasting El Niño pattern is all but certain to last for several months, forecasts suggest.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – We already knew this year’s El Niño was shaping up to be the strongest in recorded history , but now forecasters are warning that the weather pattern is only getting stronger.

In its latest discussion on Thursday, NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center said El Niño “strengthened further last month,” with “a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely” from January through March.

Multiple models have shown that El Niño is expected to continue strengthening through the end of the year.

“Chances remain high for a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950,” the latest guidance from the CPC explained . “With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed.”

Late last month, Columbia University climate scientist Azhar Ehsan, in a briefing to the media, provided a chart showing the probability of El Niño lasting until spring was “100% to 99%.”

“I wrote near-certain but it’s 100%,” he said at the time.

As it has been, NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center agrees El Niño is 100% sticking around for about six more months, though a La Niña pattern may not be too far away (denoted by the blue bar).

El Niño is on track to reach its peak in December, the latest Global Seasonal Climate Update from the World Meteorological Organization shows . The report suggests sea-surface temperatures are only expected to “increase to record levels” between now and December, according to a press release .

“El Niño doesn’t add new heat to the planet. It releases heat the ocean has already been storing beneath the surface – which is why a strong event so often becomes one of the hottest years measured (as with 2024),” WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok. “The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release.”

This strong, long-lasting El Niño is expected to have a “pretty substantial impact” on the weather we see over the next several months, Brian James, Nexstar chief meteorologist, said last month.

As we head into winter, how El Niño plays out will be very different for the northern half of the country and the southern half . Broadly speaking, the northern states will be drier and warmer than normal, while southern states will be cooler and wetter.

“Based on what I am seeing now, I am officially concerned,” Daniel Swain, a prominent climate scientist at the California Institute for Water Resources, said on social media earlier this week, as reported by Nexstar’s KTLA. “We’ve never seen an event this big before in the context of our rapidly warming climate … The warning lights are flashing.”

California has already declared a state of emergency for the impending weather pattern while crews in Los Angeles are working to prepare for its impacts .

Ehsan said in a September media briefing that this year’s atmospheric evolution looks similar to that of 1997 , when one of the strongest-ever El Niños formed. That winter was characterized by broken records and “unusual extremes,” climate researchers said in an April 1998 National Climatic Data Center report .

It was the country’s second-warmest and seventh-wettest winter since 1895, and the super-strong El Niño contributed to c haotic weather from coast to coast .

The temperature and precipitation outlooks for the rest of the year are also in line with a classic El Niño pattern.

An emerging El Niño and active Pacific hurricane season are bringing significant coastal erosion and sand loss to Southern California beaches, with experts warning the situation could worsen this winter. In addition, an oceanic Kelvin wave is moving up the coastline, while remnants of Hurricane Rachel are projected to impact the region this weekend. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)

articles.title: Asos confirms breach of customer data after hackers send rogue app notification | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The hackers alerted the fashion giant's customers through a push notification that said they had "fully compromised" the company's cloud storage.
articles.body:
U.K. fashion retail giant Asos has confirmed a data breach of its customers’ personal information after hackers used the company’s own app to notify users that the company had been compromised.

Asos said in a filing with the London Stock Exchange that hackers broke into a third-party platform hosting data that the company uses to communicate with customers.

The company said that names and contact information were taken in the breach.

BBC News reports that the stolen data includes home addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses, as well as notes relating to customer profiles, such as their website search queries.

Asos said the hackers sent an “unauthorised customer notification,” which many posted to social media. The notification addressed Asos’ data protection officer and IT department and said that the hackers “fully compromised” the company’s data hosted on Snowflake, a tech company that allows its corporate customers to analyze large amounts of data. “Engage with us, or we will leak it,” the notification reads.

By using the app’s own notification system to alert customers, the hackers are trying to pressure the company into engaging with them or risk having the stolen data published online.

The hackers reportedly broke into the Snowflake instance by “impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials,” reports Bleeping Computer . Snowflake said it had not experienced a breach of its systems. It’s unclear if the Asos-run Snowflake instance was protected with multi-factor authentication. It’s also not known how the hackers gained access to Asos’ system for sending in-app push notifications, which is often handled by a third-party service.

The hackers, who go by the handle Xuanye Group, have not indicated how much data they allegedly possess. Asos has 17 million customers, according to its website .

Earlier this year, fintech giant Betterment was compromised by hackers who used their access to the company’s third-party marketing platform to impersonate the company and send a crypto scam to its customers. The hackers also accessed customer names, email addresses, and phone numbers, among other data, during the breach.

articles.title: Top House Democrat unveils surprise medical billing overhaul
articles.summary: New legislation from Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (N.J.), the top Democrat on the powerful House Energy and Commerce Committee, aims to overhaul a key part of a law that protects patients from surprise medical bills. The new bill aims to fix what Pallone and critics say is the flawed dispute resolution system between insurers and providers.…
articles.body:
New legislation from Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (N.J.), the top Democrat on the powerful House Energy and Commerce Committee, aims to overhaul a key part of a law that protects patients from surprise medical bills.

The new bill aims to fix what Pallone and critics say is the flawed dispute resolution system between insurers and providers.

The No Surprises Act, which Pallone helped write, established an arbitration process between healthcare providers and payers when there is a payment dispute. The law allows providers to file for arbitration, where they are able to make a case for much higher payments than they could otherwise receive from health plans.

While the law keeps patients from receiving a surprise bill from an out-of-network provider, the overinflated payments get passed to them anyway through higher premiums or fewer benefits.

According to Pallone, a small number of organizations, mostly backed by private equity firms — which are buying up medical practices like anesthesiology, radiology and emergency rooms — account for the majority of disputes filed through the arbitration process.

Of the 2.5 million disputes submitted in 2025, approximately 67 percent were submitted by just 10 provider groups.

Pallone’s bill — the Lower Premiums, Faster Payments Act — will replace the arbitration system with something called “benchmarking,” which stipulates that providers would be paid at the median in-network rate for their services, adjusted for geography, even if they were out-of-network.

“The No Surprises Act has been an overwhelming success when it comes to protecting patients from surprise medical bills,” Pallone said in a statement. “[U]nfortunately the arbitration process is clearly not working. A few bad actors—largely backed by private equity—are gaming the system, creating backlogs, delaying payments, and driving up premiums.”

Under the “baseball style” arbitration process, insurers and providers each propose a rate for a given service. There’s no room for negotiation, and an arbitrator must choose one of the suggested figures.

Pallone supported the benchmarking approach from the start but compromised to get the legislation passed and signed into law. He is poised to be Energy and Commerce Committee chair next year if Democrats win the House, putting him in position to prioritize his bill.

Both providers and health plans blame each other for high consumer health costs . Providers argue arbitration is needed because insurers offer misleading and unrealistic reimbursement rates, while insurers and some consumer advocacy groups prefer benchmarking.

Pallone’s bill includes some benefits for providers, such as ensuring that they are paid within 30 days.

Passage of the No Surprises Act was heavily lobbied by all sides of the issue, and while there is some appetite among House and Senate lawmakers to revisit, those same forces will be brought to bear on any new effort in the next Congress.

articles.title: NFL urges Supreme Court to take up prediction market dispute
articles.summary: The NFL urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to take up a case over who has the authority to regulate prediction markets, arguing that wagers on the platforms should fall under state gambling laws. The league filed an amicus brief as part of a dispute between Kalshi and the state of New Jersey, which has…
articles.body:
The NFL urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to take up a case over who has the authority to regulate prediction markets, arguing that wagers on the platforms should fall under state gambling laws.

The league filed an amicus brief as part of a dispute between Kalshi and the state of New Jersey, which has asked the justices to weigh in on the issue that has produced conflicting decisions at the appellate level.

“This split of authority, and the consequent uncertainty about the regulatory oversight of sports wagering on DCMs [designated contract markets], pose a significant challenge to the NFL’s game-integrity and consumer-protection efforts,” it wrote in Thursday’s filing.

Kalshi and other prediction markets argue that the wagers they offer are financial instruments known as “swaps” and are federally regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

States, by contrast, view this as gambling and contend it should fall under their jurisdiction.

Under the Trump administration, the CFTC has weighed in on the dispute in favor of prediction markets, bringing numerous lawsuits against states that have moved to enforce their gambling laws against the platforms.

The NFL suggested Thursday there would be “less cause for concern” if the CFTC and prediction markets “were to adopt the same robust safeguards and engage in the same vigorous oversight” as state and tribal regulators and traditional sports betting.

“But that is not what is happening today,” it added.

The league argued the agency and platforms “have stuck to a more laissez-faire approach,” declining to implement a series of prohibited wagers that the NFL requires for sportsbooks and keeping the age limit at 18 rather than 21 years old.

It urged the Supreme Court to take up the case before another season goes by.

“Billions of dollars will be bet on NFL games through prediction markets each season, and any delay from the Court will result in increasing consumer harm and risk to game integrity,” the league wrote.

The NFL also suggested the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals and the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals “got it right” when they sided with the states on the issue, arguing that prediction market wagers should not be considered “swaps” under federal law.

A bipartisan group of 39 states similarly filed an amicus brief Thursday urging the Supreme Court to take up the case and backing New Jersey’s argument that states should be able to regulate prediction markets.

Kalshi said in a statement that its “top priority is the integrity of its markets,” underscoring that other major sports leagues have partnered with the company. It also pushed back on the NFL’s characterization of CFTC enforcement, arguing the agency is “actively policing sports-related markets.”

“The CFTC’s ongoing rulemaking addresses many of the NFL’s supposed concerns,” Kalshi added. “And those rules sit atop the same comprehensive system of federal enforcement that protects trillions of dollars of transactions in US markets.”

articles.title: Vance says foreign workers at Microsoft will no longer be able to apply for permanent status
articles.summary: Vice President Vance said Thursday that foreign workers at Microsoft will no longer be able to apply for permanent resident status in the U.S. through an employer-based program, after he accused the company of abusing the process. The tech giant has been suspended from the permanent labor certification program, referred to as PERM, which allows…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance said Thursday that foreign workers at Microsoft will no longer be able to apply for permanent resident status in the U.S. through an employer-based program, after he accused the company of abusing the process.

The tech giant has been suspended from the permanent labor certification program , referred to as PERM, which allows companies to hire foreign workers to work permanently in the U.S.

“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said at a press conference.

“Now, our message to Microsoft and to any other foreign or domestic corporation is quite simple,” he added. “We obviously want you to thrive in the United States of America.”

“We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector. We are the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers.”

Vance accused Microsoft of benefiting heavily from both the PERM program and H-1B visa program last year, while also laying off thousands of American workers. The H-1B visa is used to hire international talent for specialty jobs.

Microsoft argued Thursday the “vast majority” of its employees in the U.S. are Americans, adding that 80 percent of its applications to the H-1B visa program last year were to extend or change the status of existing employees.

The company’s remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the U.S., it added.

“Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” a spokesperson said in a statement. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.”

“Microsoft succeeds as a global technology leader by developing the world’s best technology workforce,” they continued. “We do this by strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world.”

Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said Thursday that Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys and several other IT firms were also suspended from the PERM program.

The Trump administration has previously taken aim at foreign hiring through the H-1B visa program, which is used to bring on international talent for specialty jobs, amid a broader push to curb immigration.

President Trump announced last year that he was raising the fee for the H-1B visa application to $100,000. The move sparked concerns in Silicon Valley, which is reliant on the program to recruit highly skilled workers from overseas.

A federal judge blocked the administration from imposing the fee in June. But the Department of Homeland Security proposed a new $103,265 fee on H-1B visas in late August.

articles.title: New York accuses TikTok of serving users ‘placebo’ safety features
articles.summary: Unsealed allegations in New York’s lawsuit against TikTok claim it ran a test that gave thousands of users a non-functional version of safety features like Algo Refresh.
articles.body: New York is alleging that thousands of TikTok users, including kids and teens, were unknowingly given “ghost” versions of the platform’s safety features rather than the working versions. Reuters reports the allegation is part of an “updated, sealed version” of New York’s 2024 lawsuit against TikTok, which was “later ordered unsealed by a judge.” According to the new allegations, TikTok’s “experiment” effectively blocked some users from accessing features like an option to reset your algorithm, which can potentially help users avoid harmful content popping up in their feed. As Reuters notes, users in the experiment “believed they had activated ​the feature, but their feeds did not change, unlike users who got the fully working version.” New York’s newly unsealed claims also allege TikTok ran other tests like this, like one Bloomberg reported earlier this year where TikTok allegedly withheld a safety update to its algorithm for some users. TikTok spokesperson Nathaniel Brown said in a statement to The Verge, “We continuously make improvements to our platform which means that, like most companies, we regularly test new products and features to validate the experience and understand how they work in the real world.” New York also claims that a product manager for Digital Well Being at TikTok internally raised concerns about the test, saying, “This feature is ​about algorithm transparency and control [...] A placebo group completely conflicts with that.” The lawsuit claims TikTok misled users about the feature, as well, presenting Algo Refresh as a permanent reset, rather than a temporary one.

articles.title: Trump administration says Microsoft ‘abused’ worker visa program and is cutting off access
articles.summary: The Trump administration is suspending some tech companies, including Microsoft, from an immigration program that lets an employer hire foreign workers and give them permanent US residency.
articles.body: The Trump administration is suspending some tech companies, including Microsoft, from an immigration program that lets an employer hire foreign workers that can reside permanently in the US, as reported by Reuters. In a press conference, Vice President JD Vance claimed the permanent labor certification program — intended for use when there aren’t “sufficient” US workers available to do a job — has become “rife” with fraud over the “past several years,” and that no company has “abused” the system more than Microsoft. “Our message to Microsoft is: you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.” The administration is also suspending companies including Adobe, Cognizant, and Infosys. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling claims Microsoft and Adobe “requested almost 3 million foreign workers,” received “over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals,” and “over 100,000 permanent labor certifications.” Vance also said Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers last year and “benefited” from 6,300 H-1B visas and “almost 3,000 green cards.” Microsoft, in a blog post responding to the suspension, said the following: > We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information. For example, of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country. > Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category. We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work. The suspensions are part of a broader crackdown on immigration from the Trump administration, including its recently-announced price hike on H-1B visas that are popular with Big Tech companies. articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln docks in San Diego after grueling deployment
articles.summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in San Diego on Thursday, completing a lengthy and grueling deployment to the Middle East, which was mired in tight food supplies and degrading mental health onboard the massive ship. The Lincoln, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, completed the 322-day deployment, which was expected to end this summer. It was extended…
articles.body:
The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in San Diego on Thursday, completing a lengthy and grueling deployment to the Middle East, which was mired in tight food supplies and degrading mental health onboard the massive ship.

The Lincoln, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, completed the 322-day deployment, which was expected to end this summer. It was extended as part of the U.S. war against Iran, in which the aircraft carrier helped enforce the U.S. naval blockade in the Arabian Sea.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth praised the crew on Wednesday for supporting the U.S. military’s operations against Iran, arguing the Abraham Lincoln strike group “projected decisive combat power and established maritime advantage” to help achieve President Trump’s strategic objectives.

“I draw inspiration from the mission that you executed so successfully,” the Pentagon chief said in a 16-minute speech aboard the vessel. “You have changed the arc of history, ensuring that crazy people, theocrats, never get a nuclear weapon, changes the arc of history.”

The Defense secretary said the Lincoln’s crew members showed resilience, conceding they operated in a tough environment, and he accused the news media of attempting to “turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale, or a symbol of a failed mission.”

“When I talk to your leadership, and I have had a chance to talk to a number of you, I know it’s the exact opposite, which is actually what the media does so often. They see success, and they see excellence, and they see difficulty and challenge that needs to be overcome, an extension, a challenging environment, and they want to point to it as a symbol of something that was missed or wrong,” Hegseth said.

For its achievements, the Defense secretary presented the highest unit award, the Presidential Unit Citation, to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group.

The strike group executed 3,693 combat sorties, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk land-attack cruise missiles, shot down 77 Iranian one-way attack drones, sunk 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 antiship cruise missiles and defended against four fast-attack craft and dhows, according to Hegseth.

The deployment of the Lincoln, with about 5,000 sailors onboard, was thrust in the news cycle following news reports of poor living conditions, food supply challenges and degrading mental health.

The aircraft carrier did not have a port call for 286 days; it finally docked in Thailand for several days last month.

Part of the reason the Lincoln ran into logistical challenges is that Iranian strikes devastated the Naval Support Activity in Bahrain, the home of the U.S. 5th Fleet and the Navy’s logistics hub in the region.

Democratic lawmakers and some former Pentagon officials criticized the lengthy deployment, arguing the administration owes answers to military families.

Rep. Mike Levin (D-Calif.), whose district includes parts of San Diego, praised the sailors as “heroes,” saying they earned their homecoming, but argued the Trump administration owes answers to military families.

“For months, Marines and Sailors sounded the alarm about conditions aboard the ship, inadequate support, and the mental health toll this deployment was taking on those serving onboard,” Levin said Thursday on social media. “Their families begged for help and were repeatedly ignored.”

“And when those families were forced to turn to the press just to be heard, Pete Hegseth responded by telling the world the reports were fake news,” Levin wrote. “That is beyond unacceptable. It’s a betrayal of the men and women who put everything on the line for this country.”

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), a Senate Armed Services Committee member, that eight sailors assigned to the Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during the deployment.

The end of the deployment for some abroad will mean they can see their family members for the first time.

“I just want to hold him, play with him,” said Brent Ledbetter, an air traffic control center officer, in an interview with NBC News when speaking about his baby boy, Nathan.

“He’s crawling around now, so I’m excited to chase him around the house and give him all the love that, that, you know —have been kind of withheld for the last 10 months,” he said. “I’m so excited.”

Hegseth told sailors on Wednesday to pass on gratitude from President Trump and himself to family members for the long wait “we believe, was in service of a righteous and historic mission.”

“Thank them for their patience, for their patriotism, for their love, and for their support for pitching in on the homeland, which is never easy.”

articles.title: In drought-hit Maharashtra, tech glitch forces teachers to fund mid-day meals
articles.summary: Maharashtra drought: PM Poshan fund delay due to SPARSH tech glitch forces teachers to pay for mid-day meals as cooks’ salaries remain pending.
articles.body: Pune: For the last four months, since the start of the academic year, teachers and headmasters across govt schools in Maharashtra have been paying from their own pockets to keep their mid-day meal programmes running. The schools, officials said, were hit by a delay in the disbursal of the PM Poshan fund, a central scheme that sponsors the meals. Even the cooks haven’t been paid salaries, teachers told TOI.In Maharashtra, the funding delay comes at a time of severe drought, across 70% of the state. Essentially, a school meal is now among the few sources of assured nutrition for tens of thousands of children as their parents struggle with falling farm incomes.A headmaster in Beed, who didn’t want to be named, said supplies of foodgrains and pulses have been coming in, but school heads have been paying for cooking fuel and vegetables since June 15. “You need more than just cauliflower or potatoes to make the meals,” he said. “You need the smaller things too, like ginger, garlic and chilli, every day. The drought has forced households to limit food options. Most of our children are only having watery dal, chutney and onion with bhakri at home. So this one school meal is the only source of good nutrition they’re now getting.”The headmaster said if he had not paid for food supplies, children would’ve dropped out of school. “But what is worse is the condition of our cooks because the funds are their only source of income. How will they live without money?”The mid-day meal became one of the most important welfare schemes in the country after evidence showed it had increased school enrollments. But the govt’s handling of the scheme has been apathetic to say the least, said Bhausaheb Chasker, a ZP teacher from Akole, Ahilyanagar. “The school heads don’t raise their voice because the administration warns them of court action. So the onus to keep the programme running is often pushed on the teachers and workers,” Chasker said.The funds issue, officials said, was triggered by delays in the adoption of the single nodal agency (SNA) SPARSH, set in place to manage direct cash transfers in centrally sponsored schemes. There were issues too in getting both central and state funds inserted into the system.“Money from the Centre for workers’ salaries has finally arrived. Centre pays Rs 600 and state pays Rs 400 per worker every month. On top of that, the state pays Rs 1,500 per worker per month extra. That also needed to be added to the system. Work is almost done and within 8-10 days the money will be disbursed. As for the funding for fuel and vegetables, that bill has been kept at the state treasury and that too will be disbursed before Dasara,” one official said.But headmasters TOI spoke to said reimbursements are often delayed. Vijay Kombe, a headmaster in Wardha, said: “For students in classes 1 to 5, the amount given is Rs 2.59 per student and for students in classes 6 to 8, it is Rs 3.71 per head. In this day and age, is that enough to buy vegetables and fuel? I pay around Rs 3000 per month to buy fuel and vegetables for 125 students in my school. We cannot put the entire responsibility on the school management committee because parents come from extremely poor backgrounds,” Kombe said.Another school official, requesting anonymity, said it was “laughable” that with the meagre amounts provided by the govt, headmasters were also expected to provide one additional nutritious item such as chikki, rajgira laddoo, apple or a banana every week.“Someone once suggested dry-fruits. Who sells dry fruits for Rs 2? Also one school gets one LPG cylinder per month. When the cylinder runs out, it’s the headmaster who has to arrange fire wood for an open stove. That’s the reality. How does govt expect one cylinder to be enough for a month? Even to book a new cylinder, we have to wait 25 days. We’re teachers who’re dealing with students from some of the poorest families in the state. It breaks our hearts if we don’t feed them,” the headmaster said.Ashok Thorat, national secretary of the Mid-Day Meal Workers’ Federation of India (MDMWFI), said workers held multiple protests to draw attention to the issue. Maharashtra employs 1.58 lakh workers under the mid-day meal scheme, which pays them Rs 83 every day for five hours of work daily. Of this, Thorat said 70% are women.“And now we can’t even pay them. All the workers come from marginalized communities. The govt keeps blaming the issue on new software so how is it that officials are getting salaries on time?” Thorat said.He added the workers have continued to come in despite the delay in salaries. “They have no choice and are scared of losing even this job. articles.title: HHS launches NIH clinic to study vaccine injuries
articles.summary: The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has launched a clinic dedicated to studying “patients experiencing health problems following vaccination” as it mulls reimbursement program for doctors who report vaccine-related injuries. HHS said the new office — located within the National Institutes of Health’s (NIH) headquarters in Bethesda — opened earlier this week, it…
articles.body:
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has launched a clinic dedicated to studying “patients experiencing health problems following vaccination” as it mulls reimbursement program for doctors who report vaccine-related injuries.

HHS said the new office — located within the National Institutes of Health’s (NIH) headquarters in Bethesda — opened earlier this week, it announced Thursday . Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the initiative is reflective of the Trump administration’s efforts to take those who report post-vaccination health problems seriously.

“We must listen to patients and families who report vaccine injuries—not dismiss or gaslight them,” Kennedy said in a statement. “President Trump and I are building a health system that takes them seriously, follows the evidence, and uses what we learn to make vaccines safer. This is how we earn back trust in our public health institutions.”

Kennedy has long claimed that vaccines are linked to a slew of adverse health effects. Throughout his tenure as HHS secretary, he has specifically peddled the widely debunked theory that vaccinations can cause autism.

During a recent keynote address at a Children’s Health Defense conference, the anti-vaccine group Kennedy previously chaired, he claimed vaccines were linked to the chronic disease epidemic. The secretary went on to link vaccines to a collection of adverse conditions, including “diabetes, death, sudden infant death syndrome, anorexia, allergic reactions, allergies, asthma [and] autoimmune diseases.”

The agency also said Wednesday it would propose reimbursement for physicians who report suspected vaccine-related injuries to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). HHS will also now require that a patient’s electronic health records be included in vaccine-related adverse event reports.

VAERS is a voluntary, self-reported system that does not independently verify reported injuries. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website includes a disclaimer that VAERS data “may contain information that is incomplete, inaccurate, coincidental, or unverifiable.”

A bust of former Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy was stolen from outside the Washington, D.C., stadium that bears his name .

In a statement, Events DC, the company that manages the stadium, said that it “learned that the bust of Robert F. Kennedy, located in a publicly accessible space on the Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Stadium grounds, was missing from its pedestal.”

“Events DC filed a police report with the Metropolitan Police Department, and the remaining pedestal has been placed in storage,” the company added, in a statement obtained by The Hill’s sister network NewsNation.

In 2024, Congress passed legislation to assist in facilitating the redevelopment of the area known as the RFK stadium site and the return of the NFL’s Washington Commanders to the nation’s capital, with the team playing in Maryland for close to three decades.

The stadium site sits on the eastern edge of the District, near the border with Maryland.

The Commanders previously pledged $2.7 billion in private investment for the redeveloped site, with D.C. saying it would invest $1.1 billion over eight years to put up a new stadium, housing and green space on the federally-owned site on the Anacostia River.

articles.title: St. Louis Fed's Musalem sees more rate hikes in the next 6 months
articles.summary: St. Louis Federal Reserve president Alberto Musalem said inflation is elevated, driven by persistent demand pressures and recurring negative supply shocks, w...
articles.body:
St. Louis Federal Reserve president Alberto Musalem said Thursday that more interest rate hikes will be needed over the next six to nine months to bring inflation down, but he didn't indicate that the central bank needs to move at its next policy meeting.

"The important thing at this point in time is to bring inflation back towards 2% in a timely manner, and it's important to contain any further broadening of inflation pressures or any second-round effects which could be coming from the negative supply shocks or the persistent demand pressures," Musalem said in a conversation with Bloomberg.

Musalem said inflation is elevated , driven by persistent demand pressures and recurring negative supply shocks, which are leading to higher energy prices .

Musalem said he typically thinks about setting a path for monetary policy somewhere between 18 months and 2 years. If "a timely manner" for lower inflation is 18 months, that suggests rates should increase further in the next six to nine months.

He said he has not prejudged the outcome of the Fed's Oct. 27-28 meeting or what he'll do at the meeting, but said, "I think that the general direction of inflation requires us to be thinking of further policy firming here."

Markets are pricing in a better-than-80% chance that the Fed holds rates steady at the end of October, while pricing in nearly 70% odds that the central bank hikes rates for a second time this year in December.

Minutes from the Fed's September policy meeting , released Wednesday, revealed that most policymakers thought another rate increase would "likely be appropriate by year end."

articles.title: ICE detainees in Georgia used the facility’s video calling software to expose the conditions inside
articles.summary: Asylum seekers at the Folkston ICE Processing Center decried Trump’s ‘deportation courts’ in a video taken behind bars.
articles.body: Four men detained at an ICE detention center in rural Georgia used the facility’s video conferencing software to expose both the conditions inside and President Donald Trump’s hostile takeover of the immigration courts. In the five-minute video, the men describe an intentionally dysfunctional legal system designed to keep them trapped in federal custody for months or years — in privately owned facilities that profit from their confinement. The video cost the men, literally and figuratively. The Folkston ICE Processing Center has a work program for detainees in which they are paid a pittance to cook, do laundry, or clean. These wages allow them to buy supplementary food in Folkston’s commissary and stay connected to people outside. “The workers here are paid $1 a day, which is just enough for a 10-minute phone call,” said Idris Makhmudov, one of the men in the video, who says he has been detained in Folkston for 27 months and counting. Makhmudov and the three other men, who are from several different countries, appear in drab, facility-issued uniforms. Their images are blurred by the low-resolution cameras on the detention center’s tablets. It’s unclear exactly how the men made the video, but it’s possible that they called someone on the outside who recorded their message to the outside world. Samantha Hamilton, an Atlanta-based immigration attorney with Asian Americans Advancing Justice, said she received a YouTube link to the video via a Signal chat. “We’ve learned that everyone in the video that was released this weekend has been put into segregation,” said Hamilton, a member of the Shut Down Folkston campaign. “They’re facing retaliation, and they were expecting that.” Since then, 45 detainees wrote an open letter further detailing the conditions at Folkston, and an estimated 73 detainees are now on a hunger strike. [Media: ICE detention isn’t supposed to be a form of punishment; its purpose is ostensibly to ensure that people in deportation proceedings show up to their hearings. But ICE facilities are virtually indistinguishable from prisons — a point the men in the video make repeatedly. Folkston, in fact, was a prison before it became an immigrant detention center. It has many of the hallmarks of prison life, including expensive communication tools that detainees are forced to rely on to talk to people on the outside. “These facilities leave people with very few options to be able to communicate with their loved ones,” said Hamilton, who has had several clients detained at Folkston. She said each “pod” of 60 to 70 detainees has access to just three or four tablets, their only connection to the outside world. Those communications come at a price. To send messages, share photos, or make phone or video calls to their loved ones, detainees at Folkston have to use GettingOut, a proprietary software owned by the prison communications company Telmate. Earlier this year, Telmate was ordered to pay $4.23 million to settle a lawsuit stemming from a 2020 data breach in which users’ information — including names, payment details, and social security numbers — was accessed. Telmate is owned by ViaPath Technologies — formerly GlobalTel*Link — which is in turn owned by American Securities, a New York City-based private equity firm. In 2021, ViaPath charged users anywhere between 18 cents to $1.10 per minute, according to data obtained by the Prison Policy Initiative. These fees add up — so much so that in 2024, the Federal Communications Commission capped the rates companies could charge inmates and detainees to 11 to 25 cents per minute depending on the size of the facility. In 2025, after Trump returned to office, the FCC voted to raise the rate cap by up to 83 percent. Detainees in ICE custody often struggle to get the money they’ve put into these systems back after being released — or, more commonly, deported. GettingOut’s terms of service state that users will lose access to their accounts after 180 days of inactivity, after which they forfeit any money deposited into their accounts. The only way to get their money back is by calling a hard-to-reach customer service line, according to a report by WVTF. Under President Joe Biden, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered Tel*Link to pay $3 million for illegally freezing and draining funds from incarcerated people’s accounts. Communications are just one way private companies make money from immigrant detention. Folkston is owned and operated by GEO Group, a publicly traded company whose stock price soared after Trump’s reelection, jumping by more than 75 percent after election day 2024. GEO has donated lavishly to Trump’s campaigns and to related political efforts, contributing $1.4 million to Trump’s super PAC in July — perhaps to show its gratitude for the $165 million it received earlier this year in government contracts. The company receives more than $1.5 million a month to run Folkston, according to a 2021 Homeland Security budget overview. The facility, which has a capacity of 780, has a guaranteed minimum occupancy of 544. Trump’s mass deportation effort, coupled with the backlogged immigration court system, has made it easy for ICE to meet its contractually agreed-upon minimum at Folkston. The men in the video allege that they and others have been there for several years, and explain that the only ways to get out are to be granted parole, bond, or asylum — or to be deported. The latter option is the likeliest now, as Trump has transformed the immigration legal system into what one detainee calls “deportation courts.” Of the 143,729 detained cases logged into Georgia immigration courts over the past year, 81 percent involved people who had no legal representation, and were therefore far less likely to be granted any form of relief, according to federal data analyzed by researchers at Syracuse University. The odds are especially low for asylum seekers. Immigration judges in Atlanta have denied 89 percent of the 2,072 asylum cases decided so far this fiscal year, compared to 63 percent in 2023. The men in the video note that Trump has overhauled the immigration system to secure favorable rulings. Since Trump’s return to office, the Department of Justice, which oversees the immigration courts, has fired over 100 judges whose decisions don’t align with the administration’s mass deportation push. At least 153 new judges have been hired in their place. These judges are far less likely to release immigrants on bond or parole, keeping them trapped in what detainees and advocates say are substandard conditions. Hamilton, the immigration attorney, said she and other members of the Shut Down Folkston coalition regularly receive reports of nearly inedible food and filthy water in the facility, including instances where detainees have found worms in the water. Because the food is ultra-processed, she said, many of her clients have gone in healthy and been released with new medical conditions, including diabetes and high blood pressure. “Most of us are asylum seekers, those who came to the United States seeking protection from political persecution and violence in their home countries,” Makhmudov, one of the men detained at Folkston, says in the video. “Many fled out of fear of becoming political prisoners in those countries — and one might say we became political prisoners in the United States simply because we are immigrants.”

articles.title: Judge Sides With Importers to Expand Trump Tariff Refund Fight

articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- A US trade judge approved class-action status for a legal fight over refunds for President Donald Trump's global tariffs, siding with importers who contend that the process will make it easier for a wider group of companies to get their money back.

US customs authorities already have fully processed almost $130 billion in refunds since the US Supreme Court declared Trump's tariffs unlawful earlier in the year. Judge Richard Eaton, in an order Thursday, certified a group lawsuit representing all importers who haven't already submitted claims for payments.

The administration had argued that importers with certain types of claims must file their own lawsuits. That prompted importers already seeking refunds to try to expand the existing litigation to cover a broader group of companies, arguing that a class action would help small businesses that don't have the resources to sue.

The case is Freestyle World Inc. v. Customs and Border Protection, 26-cv-1088, US Court of International Trade (New York).

articles.title: US Army identifies systemic breakdowns that led to DC midair collision
articles.summary: A newly released U.S. Army report identified systemic breakdowns that led to the 2025 midair collision between an American Airlines plane and an Army helicopter. Some of the families of the 67 people who died in the crash have pushed for the release of the 50-page report — obtained by Politico — which was made…
articles.body:
A newly released U.S. Army report identified systemic breakdowns that led to the 2025 midair collision between an American Airlines plane and an Army helicopter.

Some of the families of the 67 people who died in the crash have pushed for the release of the 50-page report — obtained by Politico — which was made in May.

“I have determined by a preponderance of the evidence that breakdowns across all layers of conflict management caused this accident,” Lt. Gen. Michael C. McCurry wrote in the report.

McCurry stated the “most salient contributing factor” was two broken radio transmissions, which resulted in the Army UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter, or PAT 25, not receiving “critical details” from Reagan Washington National Airport’s air traffic control tower.

He also noted “cultural lighting played a significant role in the accident,” making it “more likely than not that the crew of PAT 25 was unable to discern the aircraft lighting of” the American Airlines flight “from the urban lighting.”

This was backed by a January National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) report that also recommended a study be conducted “to identify factors that degrade communications equipment performance and adversely affect the safety of civilian and military flight operations.”

Of the recommendations, McCurry backed an NTSB recommendation for the Army to “revise the method for allocating resources to ensure the development of a robust safety management system.”

The crash occurred more than a year ago , when an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with an American Airlines flight when it was seconds away from landing at National Airport. None of the people on board either aircraft survived.

Families of Flight 5342 , an advocacy group formed by relatives of those who died in the crash, told NewsNation affiliate WDCW that “the helicopter crew faced city lights, limited visibility through night-vision goggles and interrupted radio calls.”

“The Army’s own investigation describes a system that left too little room for error and too many opportunities for a mistake to become fatal,” the group continued.

Some of the families filed a lawsuit in September 2025 against American Airlines and the federal government, alleging wrongful death and negligence.

articles.title: Trump exempts oil exploration in Arctic petroleum reserve from environmental reviews
articles.summary: The Trump administration Thursday announced it would exempt some Arctic oil and gas exploration activities from environmental reviews. The Interior Department issued a notice exempting wintertime oil and gas exploration in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska from the reviews. The exemption will apply to seismic surveys to assess where oil is located, construction of…
articles.body:
The Trump administration Thursday announced it would exempt some Arctic oil and gas exploration activities from environmental reviews.

The Interior Department issued a notice exempting wintertime oil and gas exploration in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska from the reviews.

The exemption will apply to seismic surveys to assess where oil is located, construction of temporary roads and drilling of exploration wells. These activities are often pursued in preparation for broader-scale oil production.

The administration says that its action could ultimately help oil companies access fuel more quickly. It also said that in the past, it has found that such activities would not have a significant environmental impact.

Kevin Pendergast, the Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska state director, said in a written statement that it would “allow developers to more nimbly locate energy resources in the Petroleum Reserve, ultimately increasing domestic energy supply, leading to stable energy costs and more revenue for Alaskan communities and the American public.”

However, environmental activists criticized the maneuver.

“In issuing this categorical exclusion, this administration is seeking to fast track large scale oil drilling and seismic exploration without any further environmental analysis or public input,” Earthjustice attorney Janet Bering said in a written statement. “It is cutting the public out of this decision and future decisions.”

The move comes after the administration also recently proposed to fast-track oil production in the reserve.

In 1923, then-President Harding set aside the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska as an emergency oil supply for the Navy. Since that time, drilling projects have been approved there , but environmental advocates have also raised concerns about impacts to wildlife .

The Alaska Oil and Gas Association cheered the move, saying in a written statement “We … thank the Department of the Interior and the administration for moving this common-sense action forward.”

Pentagon awards $6.3 billion contract to Raytheon for missile interceptors

The Pentagon awarded Raytheon a $6.3 billion multi-year procurement contract on Thursday to produce Standard Missile–3 Block IB (SM-3 Blk IB) interceptors.

“Our warfighters must never face a fair fight, and the SM-3 Blk IB has proven its operational superiority to dominate any adversary across the globe,” Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael P. Duffey said in a statement .

“This contract provides production certainty to our defense industrial base, breaks sub-tier manufacturing bottlenecks, and ensures that our fleets and combatant commands have the interceptors required to dominate the battle space — air, sea or land,” Duffey continued.

SM-3s can down short or medium-range ballistic missiles at sea or on land.

U.S. Navy destroyers have relied on SM-3s against Iranian ballistic missiles during the ongoing conflict.

SM-3 B variant, which was first launched in 2014, has an enhanced two-color infrared seeker , upgraded steering and propulsion that relies on short bursts to get to the target, according to Raytheon.

The contract spans five years , with two additional option years, according to the Pentagon.

“In addition, it eliminates the programmatic and supply-chain friction that constrains private-sector capacity, forcing capital allocation directly into assembly lines, solid-rocket motor suppliers and critical domestic sub-tier vendors,” the Pentagon said.

On Thursday, at the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit , President Trump awarded Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Sergey Brin, and AMD’s Lisa Su the National Medal of Science, the nation’s top science prize. Dell Technologies’ Michael Dell and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella also received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

Together, the awardees have donated nearly $6 billion to efforts tied to Trump and his administration, according to The New Republic . Alphabet and Microsoft, for example, donated to the president’s inauguration fund and White House ballroom. AMD gave to a pro-Trump Super PAC, and Michael and Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion to help fund the Trump Accounts, the administration’s savings program for children.

Nadella received his medal right after the administration indefinitely suspended Microsoft from the H-1B program, which lets U.S. companies hire skilled foreign workers.

articles.title: What to know about the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
articles.summary: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said Thursday the firing squad execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan will be open to the public, a new revelation to the first U.S. military execution in more than six decades. Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who opened fire at Fort Hood in Texas in…
articles.body:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said Thursday the firing squad execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan will be open to the public, a new revelation to the first U.S. military execution in more than six decades.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who opened fire at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, killing 13 people, is set to be put to death on Dec. 3 at 1 p.m. local time at the same military base, according to the U.S. Army.

It would mark the first U.S. military execution in more than 60 years and the first by firing squad since World War II. A Pentagon official told The Hill the execution will be livestreamed.

Hasan killed 12 soldiers and one civilian and injured 32 others in November 2009 when he used a personal handgun to open fire at the Fort Hood processing center, where troops were preparing to deploy to Afghanistan. It marks the deadliest mass shooting ever on a U.S. military installation.

During the shooting, he was heard shouting “Allahu akbar,” or “God is great.” The attack ended when he was shot four times and arrested by civilian security officers, becoming paralyzed from the waist down.

During his 2013 trial, Hasan acted as his own lawyer, saying in his opening statement that “the evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter.”

An American-born Muslim, Hasan said he had “switched sides” and carried out the shooting in response to the U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. The incident came one month before the then-soldier was scheduled to deploy to Afghanistan.

In August 2013 a military jury found Hasan guilty on all 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder, dismissing him from the Army and sentencing him to death. That ruling has since been tied up in an appeals process that finally ended in April 2025 when the Supreme Court denied his final petition .

Hasan is incarcerated in the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., and is one of just four people on military death row.

Hegseth has long made clear he wanted “the harshest lawful punishment” for Hasan, telling reporters in September 2025 that he had asked President Trump for final approval for the military execution.

“The victims and survivors deserve justice without delays,” he said in a statement to The Hill at the time.

Following Monday’s announcement that Trump had approved Hegseth’s recommendation, the Pentagon chief confirmed the execution had been set for Dec. 3 as it falls on a Thursday, the same day of the week Hasan had planned his attack.

“Of course we’re going to do it at Fort Hood. We’re going to do it on a Thursday, we’re going to do it at 1 o’clock, which is when he did it, and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad,” Hegseth told Real America’s Voice on the USS Abraham Lincoln Thursday.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” he added.

Army rules allow for at least two media outlets to be present for the execution, but no legal execution has ever been broadcast live in the U.S. The country’s last public execution was in 1936.

Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle chose death by firing squad for Hasan after Trump approved Hegseth’s recommendation, in accordance with 2023 Army regulation on how to carry out military executions.

Under the rules, the Army secretary decides the time, location and method, to take place no sooner than 60 days and no later than 150 days after the president has approved the sentence.

In this case, Hasan’s execution is to be carried out 63 days after Trump’s approval.

It also states that “all lawful and feasible methods available” for executing prisoners will be presented to the official for consideration.

There is a small chance the execution could be derailed, as Hasan could delay it if he files a habeas corpus appeal in the federal courts.

The last American service member to be put to death by firing squad was Pvt. Edward Donald Slovik, convicted of deserting his unit twice in combat in France. He was executed in the country on Jan. 31, 1945.

At the time, Slovik’s execution method was unusual, as he was the only U.S. soldier to be put to death for that reason since the Civil War. Hanging was the preferred method for most of the known U.S. military executions during WW II, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Since then, the U.S. military has carried out only one other execution with the 1961 hanging of Pvt. John Bennett for the 1955 rape and attempted murder of an Austrian girl.

articles.title: OpenAI users in Russia, Iran used models to push political agenda online, in media
articles.summary: OpenAI banned several accounts associated with two propaganda operations based in Iran and Russia, respectively, it confirmed Thursday — the latter of which the tech company said had the greatest reach it has recorded since it began reporting on and disrupting such schemes. The influence operations used OpenAI models alongside “more traditional techniques and technologies…
articles.body:
OpenAI banned several accounts associated with two propaganda operations based in Iran and Russia, respectively, it confirmed Thursday — the latter of which the tech company said had the greatest reach it has recorded since it began reporting on and disrupting such schemes.

The influence operations used OpenAI models alongside “more traditional techniques and technologies to support sophisticated ‘false front’ entities,” and in turn, covertly promote the two countries’ political agendas. The plots involved the use of AI to create and spread fake news stories, as well as operate a fraudulent think tank.

“They used those entities to launder geopolitical, conflict-related messaging into their target audiences,” OpenAI wrote. “The Iranian operation included a stable of seven ‘journalist’ personas which it used to pitch long-form articles to small and medium online outlets around the world; the Russian operation appears to have co-opted unwitting people in Latin America to run a ‘think tank’ on the ground.”

The tech firm noted that the operations were “trying a range of different tactics to achieve their goals”; the Iranian operation generated social media comments regarding the U.S.’s war with the Islamic Republic while the Russian operation created fake “leaked” documents and audio scripts — including some that “undermine[d] recruitment for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”

The Russian operation, which OpenAI referred to as “Dark Clark” after a fake persona created for the scheme, also “fed into public tensions between Ukraine and Poland.” As part of the plot, they generated reports tied to the “Social Research Center,” a faux think tank that recruited employees throughout Latin America and tricked institutions throughout the region.

The Iranian plot, dubbed “Bogus Bylines,” used virtual private networks to disguise users’ locations and generate different “American freelance writer” personas, though transparency settings located the accounts in Iran. Those running the accounts then generated false stories surrounding the U.S.-Iran war under these personas and flooded social media platforms with comments related to geopolitical topics — both in English and Persian.

“Both operations also made heavy use of AI to draft internal reports,” OpenAI added, noting that the Russian operation did this more than anything else. “In both cases, the actors used questionable or outright deceitful methodologies to exaggerate the operators’ effectiveness.”

In 2025, OpenAI similarly reported that U.S. foreign adversaries were using ChatGPT with other AI models to “ achieve their arms ,” citing another Russian cyber operation that posted AI-generated content across various platforms.

The latest report comes as the American public’s trust in AI, and in lawmakers’ ability to handle its development, dwindles. In a recent Reuters/Ipsos survey , 57 percent of respondents said they believe the Trump administration is not taking the risks posed by AI seriously enough, while 54 percent said the same of Congress.

The Trump administration has largely favored voluntary safeguards over sweeping federal regulations.

President Trump invited key AI industry leaders to the White House last week, where the CEOs for tech firms such as Nvidia, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceXAI agreed to a “ morally-binding ” self-policing pledge that involved a series of safety measures, including external reviews of their AI systems. However, critics say they don’t trust these companies to self-regulate.

OpenAI stated that reporting on AI-based influence operations like those exposed Thursday will hopefully make “further research and disruption” easier for the company to prevent similar schemes in the future, adding that these reports have in some cases deterred such activity.
